emt-pharm-l01.q: A well-perfused patient swallows a tablet. About how long until it takes effect?
choices: 1 to 3 minutes
5 to 10 minutes
30 to 60 minutes
2 to 4 hours
emt-pharm-l01.why: Oral is the slowest route an EMT deals with, roughly 30 to 60 minutes, because the drug has to survive the stomach and pass through the liver first. The 1 to 3 minute figure is sublingual and 5 to 10 minutes is intramuscular.

emt-pharm-l01.q: A patient tells you she takes no aspirin, only Ecotrin for her heart. What is the correct conclusion?
choices: Ecotrin is a trade name for aspirin, so she is taking aspirin
Ecotrin is a nitrate and unrelated to aspirin
She takes neither, since Ecotrin is a vitamin
Ecotrin is an aspirin substitute with no bleeding risk
emt-pharm-l01.why: Ecotrin, Bayer and St. Joseph are all trade names for acetylsalicylic acid. Patients report the brand on the bottle, which is why you chart the generic name and read the label yourself.

emt-pharm-l02.q: When are the three label checks performed?
choices: Once at the start of shift, once at the hospital, once at the station
When you take it from the bag, when you prepare it, and immediately before it enters the patient
Three times in a row right before administration
Only when a partner is available to watch
emt-pharm-l02.why: The three checks are spaced across the sequence so a mistake made at one step gets caught at the next. Three rapid looks at the same moment repeat the same error three times.

emt-pharm-l02.q: Your partner, another EMT, gives the medication while you direct the care. What is this called?
choices: Patient-assisted administration
Peer-assisted administration
Offline medical direction
Independent practice
emt-pharm-l02.why: Peer-assisted means another provider or a family member administers under your direction. Patient-assisted is when the patient takes it themselves with your coaching, and offline direction describes the written protocol, not who pushes the drug.

emt-pharm-l03.q: A nasal cannula is running at 4 L/min. Approximately what oxygen concentration is the patient receiving?
choices: About 24 to 44%
About 60 to 70%
About 80 to 90%
Near 100%
emt-pharm-l03.why: A nasal cannula at 1 to 6 L/min delivers roughly 24 to 44%. The 80 to 90% range belongs to a nonrebreather at 10 to 15 L/min, and near 100% requires a bag-valve mask with a reservoir.

emt-pharm-l03.q: An alert 55-year-old with chest pain has a room-air saturation of 97% and no respiratory distress. What oxygen is indicated?
choices: 15 L/min by nonrebreather for all chest pain
6 L/min by simple mask
2 L/min by nasal cannula as a precaution
None; he is already in the 94 to 98% target range
emt-pharm-l03.why: Oxygen treats hypoxia, and 97% is already inside the 94 to 98% target. Routine high-flow oxygen for every chest-pain patient is an outdated habit the exam offers deliberately as a distractor.

emt-pharm-l04.q: Your kit holds only 81 mg chewable aspirin. How many tablets make the prehospital dose?
choices: Two
Three
Four
Eight
emt-pharm-l04.why: 324 mg divided by 81 mg is four chewable tablets. Two tablets is 162 mg and eight would be 648 mg, double the intended dose.

emt-pharm-l04.q: A 9-year-old has a fever and body aches from a viral illness. Why is aspirin withheld?
choices: Aspirin has no antifever effect in children
Risk of Reye syndrome, which damages the liver and brain
Children cannot chew tablets
Aspirin raises blood pressure in children
emt-pharm-l04.why: Aspirin given to a child or teenager with a fever or viral illness is linked to Reye syndrome. Aspirin does lower fever and children can chew, so the contraindication is about the syndrome, not the mechanics.

emt-pharm-l05.q: A 30-year-old has hives over both arms after a bee sting. Her chest is clear, she speaks in full sentences, and her BP is 128/80. Is epinephrine indicated?
choices: Yes, any hives after a sting is anaphylaxis
Yes, give 0.15 mg because the reaction is mild
No; there is no respiratory or circulatory involvement, so this is not anaphylaxis
No, because hives are never an allergic sign
emt-pharm-l05.why: Anaphylaxis requires respiratory compromise, hypotension, or two or more body systems involved. Isolated hives with normal breathing and pressure is an allergic reaction that is monitored and transported, not an epinephrine call.

emt-pharm-l05.q: A patient treated with epinephrine feels completely normal 20 minutes later and wants to stay home. Why do you push for transport?
choices: The epinephrine must be monitored for 24 hours by law
A biphasic reaction can return 4 to 12 hours later after the epinephrine wears off
Epinephrine causes delayed hypoglycemia
The auto-injector needle requires a hospital dressing
emt-pharm-l05.why: Epinephrine lasts far less time than the immune cascade it interrupted, so symptoms can return hours later when nobody is there. Feeling well on scene is exactly the presentation that gets people into trouble.

emt-pharm-l06.q: You are using an atomizer with a naloxone syringe rather than a prefilled nasal device. What is the standard total dose and split?
choices: 4 mg total, all in one nostril
2 mg total, 1 mg per nostril
0.4 mg total, split between nostrils
10 mg total, 5 mg per nostril
emt-pharm-l06.why: The atomizer approach gives 2 mg total, 1 mg per nostril, so each side has enough surface area to absorb. The 4 mg single-nostril figure belongs to the prefilled commercial device.

emt-pharm-l06.q: Medical direction orders activated charcoal at 1 g/kg for an alert 30 kg child. What do you do with the calculated number?
choices: Give 30 g without further thought
Give 300 g, since pediatric doses are scaled up
Calculate 30 g, then check it against the 12.5 to 25 g pediatric protocol range and confirm with the physician
Give 3 g, because children get one tenth of the adult dose
emt-pharm-l06.why: The 1 g/kg formula gives 30 g, but the usual pediatric range is 12.5 to 25 g, so the calculation is a starting point you reconcile with protocol. Blindly giving a calculated number that exceeds the protocol range is how overdoses happen.

emt-pharm-l07.q: After a metered-dose inhaler puff, how long should the patient hold the breath and how long before the next puff?
choices: Hold 2 seconds, next puff immediately
Hold 10 seconds, wait about 1 minute
Hold 30 seconds, wait 5 minutes
No hold is needed, wait 10 seconds
emt-pharm-l07.why: Holding about 10 seconds lets the drug settle onto the airway lining instead of being exhaled, and roughly a minute between puffs lets the first one open the airway so the second gets deeper. Firing puffs back to back wastes the second one.

emt-pharm-l07.q: An asthmatic who was wheezing loudly ten minutes ago now has almost no breath sounds but is tripoding and cannot speak. What does this mean?
choices: The albuterol worked and the attack is resolving
Too little air is moving to make sound; this is impending respiratory failure
The stethoscope is being placed incorrectly
He has developed pneumonia
emt-pharm-l07.why: Wheezing requires airflow, so a quiet chest in a patient still working hard means airflow has nearly stopped. Improvement looks like easier work and better speech, not silence with worse distress.

emt-pharm-l08.q: Which diabetes medication, taken alone, rarely causes hypoglycemia?
choices: Glyburide
Glipizide
Metformin
Insulin glargine
emt-pharm-l08.why: Metformin reduces liver glucose output but does not force insulin release, so on its own it seldom drops sugar dangerously. Sulfonylureas like glyburide and glipizide, and any insulin, routinely do.

emt-pharm-l08.q: An 80-year-old on digoxin reports nausea, vomiting and yellow-green halos around lights. Her pulse is 48 and irregular. What should you suspect?
choices: Digoxin toxicity
A migraine with aura
Nitroglycerin overdose
Acute angle-closure glaucoma
emt-pharm-l08.why: Digoxin has a narrow safe range, and the classic toxic picture is gastrointestinal upset, yellow-green visual halos, confusion and a slow or irregular rhythm. A migraine aura does not slow the pulse, and she is not on nitroglycerin.

emt-pharm-l09.q: A patient weighs 190 lb. Using the field estimate of halving and subtracting 10 percent, about what weight do you use?
choices: About 68 kg
About 85 kg
About 95 kg
About 418 kg
emt-pharm-l09.why: Half of 190 is 95, minus 10 percent is about 85 kg, which is close to the exact 86.4 kg. The 95 figure is the halving step without the correction, and 418 is multiplying by 2.2 instead of dividing.

emt-pharm-l09.q: In a radio request for a medication order, which element comes last?
choices: Your unit and certification level
The patient's age, sex and chief complaint
Vital signs, history, allergies and medications
The specific request: drug, dose and route
emt-pharm-l09.why: The specific ask goes at the end so the physician has the picture before the request. Leading with the drug name makes the physician stop you and back up through the history anyway.

emt-pharm-l10.q: A patient on furosemide and digoxin has been vomiting for two days. Why is he at higher risk of digoxin toxicity?
choices: Furosemide chemically binds digoxin
Furosemide and vomiting deplete potassium, and low potassium makes the heart more sensitive to digoxin
Vomiting concentrates digoxin in the stomach
Digoxin cannot be absorbed without furosemide
emt-pharm-l10.why: Loop diuretics and vomiting both dump potassium, and a low potassium level lets a previously stable digoxin dose become toxic. The drugs do not bind each other, and the problem is the electrolyte, not absorption.

emt-pharm-l10.q: An unresponsive patient drank alcohol, took alprazolam and used heroin. After two naloxone doses his respirations improve only from 4 to 8 per minute. What is the best interpretation?
choices: The naloxone was expired and should be discarded
The opioid piece is partially reversed, but alcohol and the benzodiazepine still depress breathing; keep ventilating
He needs naloxone for the benzodiazepine as well
The pinpoint pupils rule out any non-opioid cause
emt-pharm-l10.why: Naloxone only reverses opioids, so a partial response in a polysubstance overdose is expected and does not mean the dose failed. Continued bag-valve-mask ventilation is the treatment while you look for other causes.

emt-pharm-l11.q: A patient on clozapine for schizophrenia has a temperature of 101.6 F and a sore throat. Why is this more than a routine complaint?
choices: Clozapine can wipe out white blood cells, so a fever may signal a life-threatening infection
Clozapine causes fever as a normal side effect that needs no workup
Fever makes clozapine ineffective but is otherwise harmless
Clozapine patients cannot be transported for fever
emt-pharm-l11.why: Clozapine can cause severe loss of infection-fighting white cells, so fever in these patients is treated as an emergency rather than a nuisance. Dismissing it as a drug side effect is the dangerous answer.

emt-pharm-l11.q: You find buprenorphine-naloxone films and a pharmacy log for daily methadone dosing. What does this tell you about a possible overdose today?
choices: This patient cannot overdose on opioids
Naloxone is contraindicated in these patients
Tolerance is high and naloxone works poorly against buprenorphine, so expect to ventilate and repeat doses
Methadone wears off faster than naloxone, so one dose is enough
emt-pharm-l11.why: Buprenorphine binds the receptor tightly so standard naloxone doses may barely shift it, and methadone outlasts naloxone by many hours. Ventilation is the constant, and repeat dosing plus transport is the plan.

emt-pharm-l12.q: Medical direction wants 25 g of dextrose delivered as D10. What volume is that?
choices: 25 mL
50 mL
100 mL
250 mL
emt-pharm-l12.why: D10 is 10 g per 100 mL, or 0.1 g/mL, so 25 g requires 250 mL. The 50 mL answer is the D50 volume, which carries the same grams in one tenth the fluid.

emt-pharm-l12.q: How many grams of sodium chloride are in a 1,000 mL bag of 0.9% normal saline?
choices: 9 g
emt-pharm-l12.why: A percent solution is grams per 100 mL, so 0.9% is 0.9 g per 100 mL and 1,000 mL holds ten times that, which is 9 g. Reading 0.9% as 0.9 g per bag is the common slip.

emt-pharm-l13.q: A 12 kg toddler has anaphylaxis. Your protocol authorizes drawing from a 1 mg/mL vial at 0.01 mg/kg. What dose and volume?
choices: 0.12 mg, which is 0.12 mL
0.12 mg, which is 1.2 mL
0.3 mg, which is 0.3 mL
1.2 mg, which is 1.2 mL
emt-pharm-l13.why: 0.01 mg/kg times 12 kg is 0.12 mg, and from a 1 mg/mL vial that is 0.12 mL. The 1.2 mL answers move the decimal a full place, a tenfold error, and 0.3 mg is the adult device dose.

emt-pharm-l13.q: A severe asthmatic has had two albuterol treatments with no improvement and is barely moving air. Some protocols now allow which medication?
choices: Oral glucose 15 g
Activated charcoal 25 g
Intramuscular epinephrine 0.3 mg
Sublingual nitroglycerin 0.4 mg
emt-pharm-l13.why: Epinephrine stimulates the same beta-2 receptors albuterol targets, and by the intramuscular route it reaches airways that inhaled drug can no longer get to. It varies by protocol, but none of the other three treat bronchospasm.

emt-pharm-l14.q: A 28-week pregnant patient has an opioid overdose with a respiratory rate of 5. How is naloxone used?
choices: Withhold naloxone entirely; only ventilate
Give the maximum dose immediately to protect the fetus
Ventilate and titrate to adequate breathing only, since full reversal can trigger fetal withdrawal and preterm labor
Give naloxone orally to slow absorption
emt-pharm-l14.why: The fetus depends on the mother's oxygenation, so you ventilate and give just enough naloxone to restore breathing. Full reversal can precipitate fetal withdrawal and preterm labor, and withholding it entirely leaves the mother hypoxic.

emt-pharm-l14.q: Why might a patient who overdosed on buprenorphine respond poorly to a standard naloxone dose?
choices: Buprenorphine is not an opioid
Buprenorphine binds the receptor very tightly, so standard doses may barely displace it
Naloxone is destroyed by buprenorphine
Buprenorphine has a shorter half-life than naloxone
emt-pharm-l14.why: Buprenorphine has an unusually strong grip on the opioid receptor, so naloxone struggles to push it off at normal doses. It is very much an opioid, and it lasts longer than naloxone, not shorter.

emt-pharm-l15.q: A 32-year-old with crushing chest pain admits to using cocaine an hour ago. His BP is 168/96. What is true about nitroglycerin?
choices: It is absolutely contraindicated after cocaine use
It is genuinely helpful, because cocaine constricts coronary arteries
It must be doubled to overcome the cocaine
It converts cocaine into a more toxic compound
emt-pharm-l15.why: Cocaine causes coronary vasoconstriction, and nitroglycerin dilates those vessels, so it is one of the settings where the drug directly addresses the mechanism. The pressure is high, so the usual systolic gate is easily met.

emt-pharm-l15.q: A chest-pain patient says aspirin gives him heartburn. How should you classify that?
choices: A true allergy, so withhold aspirin
An intolerance, not an allergy; aspirin is still indicated unless a real contraindication exists
Evidence of aspirin-exacerbated respiratory disease
A reason to give half the dose
emt-pharm-l15.why: Heartburn is a side effect, not an immune reaction. Hives, facial swelling or wheezing after aspirin would be a true allergy, and asthma with nasal polyps plus prior NSAID wheezing is the pattern that genuinely rules it out.

emt-pharm-l16.q: What is the intramuscular glucagon dose for an adult, and how fast does it work?
choices: 0.1 mg, onset under 1 minute
1 mg, onset 8 to 15 minutes
5 mg, onset 2 minutes
15 g, onset 30 minutes
emt-pharm-l16.why: Glucagon is 1 mg IM for patients about 25 kg and up, with onset around 8 to 15 minutes, which is slow when the brain has no fuel. The 15 g figure is the oral glucose tube, a different drug entirely.

emt-pharm-l16.q: A sweaty, confused diabetic's continuous sensor reads 88 mg/dL. What should you do?
choices: Trust the sensor and look for another cause
Confirm with a fingerstick, because sensors lag capillary glucose by 5 to 15 minutes during a fast fall
Recalibrate the sensor before treating
Give 15 g of oral glucose only if the sensor drops below 70
emt-pharm-l16.why: Sensors read the fluid between cells, so during a rapid drop the displayed number is minutes behind the blood. A fingerstick settles it, and the symptomatic patient is treated based on the patient and the confirmed value.

emt-pharm-l17.q: Four layers must all say yes before you can give a medication as an EMT. Which list is correct?
choices: National scope model, state law, your medical director's protocol, and your own current credential
Your partner, your supervisor, the hospital, and the patient
The manufacturer, the pharmacy, the state, and the patient's insurance
National scope model alone, since it is the federal standard
emt-pharm-l17.why: The national scope is a floor, the state writes the actual list, the medical director's protocol puts it in your bag with an indication and dose, and you must hold the credential. Any one of the four saying no ends it.

emt-pharm-l17.q: Which of these is a common expanded-scope addition for nausea in EMS systems that authorize it?
choices: Activated charcoal 50 g
Ondansetron 4 mg dissolving tablet
Nitroglycerin 0.4 mg sublingual
Glucagon 1 mg intramuscular
emt-pharm-l17.why: Ondansetron as a 4 mg orally dissolving tablet is a frequent expansion for nausea and vomiting. Glucagon is an expansion too, but it treats hypoglycemia, and charcoal and nitroglycerin address entirely different problems.

emt-pharm-l18.q: An EMT has been skipping the third label check for months because it has never caused a problem. Under just culture, this is which category?
choices: Human error, which calls for consoling
At-risk behavior, which calls for coaching and removing the incentive to cut the corner
Reckless behavior, which calls for discipline
Not a behavior issue at all
emt-pharm-l18.why: Drifting into a normalized shortcut is at-risk behavior, handled with coaching and a system fix. Human error is a one-off slip, and reckless behavior means knowingly disregarding a substantial risk, like working impaired.

emt-pharm-l18.q: Which is the correct way to write a dose on a chart?
choices: .3 mg
0.3 mg
emt-pharm-l18.why: Always use a leading zero and never a trailing one. A missing leading zero can be read as 3 mg and a trailing zero as 0.30 read quickly can become 30, both tenfold or hundredfold errors.

quiz.q: A hypotensive patient in shock has a medication placed under the tongue and another rubbed into the skin. Which is more likely to work, and why?
choices: The sublingual route, because it absorbs into veins directly rather than depending on peripheral blood flow
The skin route, because skin absorbs fastest
Neither, because all routes fail in shock
Both equally, because absorption does not depend on perfusion
quiz.why: Shock shunts blood away from skin and gut, so transdermal and oral routes stall. Sublingual tissue drains straight into venous return and still works reasonably, which is why the emergency routes are IV, IM, IN, inhaled and sublingual.

quiz.q: A patient develops a pounding headache after nitroglycerin. Which term describes this?
choices: An untoward effect
A side effect
A contraindication
An indication
quiz.why: A side effect is an expected extra effect of a correctly given drug, and the nitroglycerin headache is the textbook example. An untoward effect is harmful and unexpected, and a contraindication is a reason not to give it at all.

quiz.q: Naloxone's half-life is about 30 to 90 minutes and methadone's is far longer. What does this predict?
choices: Methadone will be cleared before naloxone wears off
Naloxone will need to be reversed with an antidote
The patient may become re-sedated and stop breathing after the naloxone fades
The patient can safely refuse transport once alert
quiz.why: When the antagonist clears before the agonist, the opioid reoccupies the receptor and respiratory depression returns. That mismatch is exactly why a reversed patient who refuses transport is a high-risk refusal.

quiz.q: In a chaotic scene you are handed a medication box by a bystander who says it is the patient's. Which right does taking it at face value most directly threaten?
choices: Right documentation
Right time
Right route
Right patient and right medication
quiz.why: An unverified box may be the wrong drug or prescribed to someone else, which attacks both the right patient and the right medication. Route, time and documentation are all downstream of confirming what the drug is and whose it is.

quiz.q: Medical direction gives you a verbal order that includes a dose you do not recognize. What is the professional response?
choices: Repeat the order back and state your concern with the specific number on the recorded line before acting
Refuse the order and terminate the call
Give the ordered dose, since the physician carries the liability
Give half of the ordered dose as a compromise
quiz.why: The read-back exists so errors surface before administration, and naming the number with your concern is the mechanism. Silently giving it, silently refusing, or inventing a middle dose all skip the check that protects the patient.

quiz.q: An EMT carries albuterol on the unit and administers it under standing orders. A second patient uses her own prescribed inhaler with the EMT's coaching. Which labels apply?
choices: Assisting for both
Administering for the first, patient-assisted for the second
Peer-assisted for the first, administering for the second
Administering for both, because the EMT is present
quiz.why: Administering means giving a drug your service carries under your scope. Assisting means helping a patient take their own prescribed medication, and when the patient does it herself with your coaching it is patient-assisted.

quiz.q: A 62-year-old with COPD arrives on home oxygen at 2 L/min with a saturation of 86% and severe distress. What is the appropriate action?
choices: Remove all oxygen to preserve respiratory drive
Place a nonrebreather at 15 L/min and leave it there
Increase oxygen and titrate to a saturation of 88 to 92%
Wait for ALS before adjusting the flow
quiz.why: An 86% saturation is hypoxia and must be treated, but COPD patients are titrated to 88 to 92% rather than flooded. Removing oxygen from a hypoxic patient and locking a nonrebreather at 15 L/min are the two opposite errors.

quiz.q: A patient pulled from a burning basement is confused with a pulse oximeter reading of 98%. What does the reading mean?
choices: Oxygenation is adequate and no oxygen is needed
The patient is hyperventilating and needs a paper bag
The oximeter is broken and should be replaced
The oximeter cannot distinguish carbon monoxide from oxygen on hemoglobin, so the reading is falsely reassuring
quiz.why: Carboxyhemoglobin reads like oxyhemoglobin on a standard pulse oximeter, so a normal number in a fire victim proves nothing. The treatment is 15 L/min by nonrebreather regardless of the displayed saturation.

quiz.q: Fifteen minutes after oral glucose, a diabetic's mental status has not improved and the repeat glucose is 43 mg/dL. He can still swallow. What is the best next step?
choices: Repeat oral glucose per protocol, request ALS, and continue to monitor the airway
Give nothing further and transport quietly
Lay him flat and administer aspirin
Give a second tube deep in the throat to speed absorption
quiz.why: Repeat dosing per protocol is appropriate while he can still protect his airway, and the failure to improve is itself a reason to escalate to ALS for IV dextrose. Placing gel deep in the throat invites aspiration.

quiz.q: Which oxygen device paired with its flow rate is correctly matched?
choices: Nonrebreather at 4 L/min
Nebulizer driven at 6 to 8 L/min
Nasal cannula at 12 L/min
Simple face mask at 2 L/min
quiz.why: A nebulizer needs 6 to 8 L/min to generate usable mist. A nonrebreather requires 10 to 15 L/min to keep the reservoir inflated, a cannula tops out near 6 L/min, and a simple mask needs at least 6 L/min to flush exhaled carbon dioxide.

quiz.q: A 70-year-old with substernal pressure has a BP of 92/58 and takes no PDE-5 inhibitors. Aspirin has been given. What about nitroglycerin?
choices: Give 0.4 mg since there is no drug interaction
Give 0.8 mg to overcome the low pressure
Withhold it; the systolic is below the usual 100 mmHg threshold
Give it only if the patient stands up first
quiz.why: Nitroglycerin lowers preload and therefore pressure, so a systolic of 92 is below the typical 100 mmHg gate in most protocols. The absence of a PDE-5 inhibitor removes one contraindication but not the hypotension.

quiz.q: Which chest-pain patient is the strongest candidate to have aspirin withheld?
choices: A 58-year-old who took a daily 81 mg aspirin this morning
A 66-year-old on apixaban for atrial fibrillation
A 71-year-old with a history of stroke ten years ago from a clot
A 49-year-old vomiting bright red blood with a known bleeding ulcer
quiz.why: Active gastrointestinal bleeding is a genuine contraindication. Daily low-dose aspirin does not block the acute dose, anticoagulated patients still receive aspirin in most protocols, and an old clot-type stroke is not the bleeding kind.

quiz.q: A patient's chest pain resolves completely after the second nitroglycerin dose. What is the correct course?
choices: Stop further doses, reassess vitals and pain, and continue transport with monitoring
Give the third dose anyway to complete the series
Cancel transport since the pain resolved
Give aspirin only now that the pain is gone
quiz.why: The maximum of three doses is a ceiling, not a target, so relief ends the dosing. Resolved pain does not mean resolved infarct, so transport and monitoring continue, and aspirin should already have been given.

quiz.q: A 19-year-old is stung by a wasp, becomes hoarse, and develops facial swelling with a BP of 88/52. He has asthma and takes propranolol. What is the correct action?
choices: Withhold epinephrine because propranolol is a contraindication
Give epinephrine 0.3 mg IM in the thigh and prepare for a repeat dose
Give albuterol only, since he is asthmatic
Give 0.15 mg because the beta blocker amplifies epinephrine
quiz.why: There is no absolute contraindication to epinephrine in true anaphylaxis, and a beta blocker only makes one dose more likely to be insufficient. Albuterol alone does nothing for the hypotension or airway swelling.

quiz.q: You are about to use an epinephrine auto-injector on a struggling 5-year-old. Which action is most likely to cause injury?
choices: Injecting through clothing
Holding the device at 90 degrees
Injecting without immobilizing the leg
Massaging the site afterward
quiz.why: A spring-loaded needle in a moving limb is how thigh lacerations happen, so the leg is held still first. Injecting through clothing, using a 90 degree angle and massaging afterward are all correct technique.

quiz.q: A 35 kg 10-year-old has anaphylaxis. Your kit holds 0.15 mg and 0.3 mg auto-injectors. Which do you use?
choices: 0.15 mg, because she is a child
Neither; wait for ALS to dose by weight
Two 0.15 mg devices in the same thigh
0.3 mg, because she is at or above 30 kg
quiz.why: The adult device applies at 30 kg and above regardless of age, and 35 kg clears that. Underdosing a child in anaphylaxis because she looks small is the error the weight bands exist to prevent.

quiz.q: A peanut-allergic teenager vomits repeatedly, becomes dizzy, and has a BP of 80/44 with completely clear skin. What is the correct interpretation?
choices: This is anaphylaxis with gastrointestinal and circulatory involvement; give epinephrine
This cannot be anaphylaxis without hives
This is a vasovagal faint; lay her flat and monitor
This is food poisoning; transport without medication
quiz.why: About one in five anaphylactic reactions has no skin findings, and vomiting plus hypotension after a known exposure is two body systems. Waiting for a rash before treating is a fatal habit.

quiz.q: An unresponsive patient has a respiratory rate of 4, pinpoint pupils, and a fentanyl patch on the right upper arm. After ventilating, which additional step matters?
choices: Leave the patch in place so the hospital can see it
Remove the patch with a gloved hand and check for additional patches
Cut the patch in half to reduce the dose
Apply a second patch to balance absorption
quiz.why: A patch keeps delivering drug, and patients sometimes wear several. Removing it with gloves stops the ongoing dose and protects you, while leaving it on means fighting a source you could have removed.

quiz.q: Which poisoning is activated charcoal least likely to help?
choices: An acetaminophen tablet overdose 30 minutes ago in an alert patient
An aspirin overdose 45 minutes ago in an alert patient
An ethylene glycol ingestion
A tricyclic antidepressant ingestion 20 minutes ago in an alert patient
quiz.why: Charcoal does not adsorb alcohols, metals, caustics or hydrocarbons, and ethylene glycol is an alcohol. The other three are tablet ingestions within the roughly one-hour window in patients who can protect the airway.

quiz.q: A patient who received naloxone is breathing 14 times a minute with good chest rise but is drowsy. Your partner wants to give more so the patient can sign a refusal. What is the correct response?
choices: Agree, since a signed refusal saves a transport
Give one more dose but not two
Give more naloxone and then let him walk to a friend's house
Decline; the endpoint is adequate ventilation, and dosing toward a refusal is both a clinical and a legal error
quiz.why: Naloxone is titrated to breathing, and pushing to full alertness causes withdrawal, vomiting and combativeness. Deliberately dosing to obtain a refusal also leaves a patient who will re-sedate when the naloxone fades.

quiz.q: A COPD patient in distress is placed on CPAP at 8 cm H2O. Six minutes later he is more alert, his work of breathing has dropped, and his systolic fell from 148 to 118. What should you do?
choices: Continue CPAP and keep monitoring; this is a response, not a failure
Remove CPAP immediately because of the pressure drop
Increase to 20 cm H2O to speed improvement
Switch to a nonrebreather to protect the blood pressure
quiz.why: A modest pressure drop is expected because positive pressure reduces venous return, and the patient is clinically better. Failure criteria are declining mental status, vomiting, hypotension or no improvement in 5 to 10 minutes.

quiz.q: Which finding after a nebulized albuterol treatment should most concern you?
choices: A heart rate rise from 92 to 118
Increasing drowsiness with a rising carbon dioxide level
Fine tremor of the hands
Complaint of a dry mouth
quiz.why: Tachycardia, tremor and dry mouth are predictable beta effects of albuterol. Rising drowsiness in a patient who was fighting to breathe signals failing ventilation and is a reason to prepare to bag, not to reassure.

quiz.q: A patient hands you a glucometer reading of 118 mg/dL taken two hours after lunch. What does that value mean?
choices: It is dangerously low and requires oral glucose
It is diagnostic of diabetic ketoacidosis
It is within normal limits for a random reading
It cannot be interpreted without a fasting sample
quiz.why: A normal random glucose stays under about 140 mg/dL, so 118 is unremarkable. Most protocols treat symptomatic hypoglycemia below 60 to 70 mg/dL, far from this number.

quiz.q: A trauma patient on metoprolol has a heart rate of 82, a BP of 104/68, cool mottled skin and a capillary refill of 4 seconds. How should you triage his condition?
choices: Stable, because the heart rate and pressure are acceptable
Hypoglycemic until proven otherwise
Having a medication reaction to metoprolol
In compensated shock; the beta blocker prevents the tachycardia you would otherwise see
quiz.why: Beta blockade prevents the compensatory rate increase, so skin signs, mental status and capillary refill become the perfusion evidence. A reassuring heart rate in a bleeding patient on a beta blocker is a trap, not a reprieve.

quiz.q: Which medication list finding most changes your urgency after a ground-level fall with a forehead laceration and a normal neurologic exam?
choices: Warfarin
Levothyroxine
Atorvastatin
Omeprazole
quiz.why: Warfarin means a bleed inside the skull will not self-limit and may declare itself hours later, so a normal exam on scene does not clear the patient. The other three do not change bleeding risk.

quiz.q: A patient's bottles include furosemide, spironolactone, metoprolol and lisinopril. She is short of breath with crackles and swollen ankles. What does the combination most support?
choices: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease
Heart failure with fluid overload
Type 1 diabetes
Seizure disorder
quiz.why: That four-drug pattern is the standard heart failure regimen, and crackles with dependent swelling fits fluid overload. None of those drugs treat airway disease, diabetes or seizures.

quiz.q: You must give 0.5 mg of a drug supplied at 2 mg/mL. What volume do you draw?
choices: 1 mL
0.5 mL
4 mL
quiz.why: Volume equals dose divided by concentration, so 0.5 divided by 2 is 0.25 mL. Answering 0.5 mL treats the label as 1 mg/mL, and 4 mL inverts the division.

quiz.q: A 27 lb toddler needs a weight-based dose. What weight do you use, and what should you do if a scale is unavailable?
choices: About 6 kg; halve the pounds
About 27 kg; estimate by appearance
About 59 kg; multiply by 2.2
About 12 kg; use a length-based resuscitation tape to confirm
quiz.why: 27 divided by 2.2 is about 12 kg, and a length-based tape gives weight plus doses and equipment sizes when no scale exists. Multiplying by 2.2 or simply halving the pounds both produce dangerous numbers.

quiz.q: Which documentation entry for a medication is complete?
choices: 1418 nitroglycerin 0.4 mg SL, patient's own, per Dr. Ruiz; 1423 pain 5/10, BP 126/78
Gave nitro, patient felt better
Nitroglycerin given en route per protocol
0.4 mg SL nitroglycerin, patient tolerated well
quiz.why: A complete entry carries drug, dose, route, time, authorization and a timed reassessment. The other entries omit the time, the authority, or the measured response, which is the part that proves the medication was monitored.

quiz.q: A patient on sertraline began taking dextromethorphan cough syrup. He is agitated and sweating with a temperature of 102.1 F, a heart rate of 130, and rhythmic ankle jerking. Over what time frame did this most likely develop?
choices: Over several days to a week
Over several hours
Over several weeks
Within seconds of the first dose
quiz.why: Serotonin syndrome builds over hours and features clonus and hyperreflexia. Neuroleptic malignant syndrome, its lookalike from antipsychotics, builds over days and shows lead-pipe rigidity with slowed reflexes instead.

quiz.q: A diabetic on carvedilol becomes unconscious with almost no warning signs beforehand. Which effect best explains the missing warning?
choices: Carvedilol prevents sweating, the only warning sign
Carvedilol raises blood sugar and masks the diagnosis
Beta blockade removed the tremor and pounding heart that normally warn of low sugar
Beta blockers cannot affect hypoglycemia symptoms
quiz.why: Beta blockade removes the adrenaline warning signs of hypoglycemia, so patients skip the tremor and palpitations. Sweating is driven by a different nerve pathway and survives the block, which is why a sweaty patient on a beta blocker gets a glucose check.

quiz.q: A patient on phenelzine for depression ate aged cheese and cured meats at a party and now has a severe headache with a systolic of 218. What is the mechanism?
choices: An allergic reaction to the food
Serotonin syndrome from the cheese
Dehydration from the salt in the meats
Blocked breakdown of norepinephrine, so the dietary surge causes a hypertensive crisis
quiz.why: MAO inhibitors block the enzyme that clears norepinephrine, so tyramine-rich foods and sympathomimetics produce a surge with nowhere to go. Serotonin syndrome comes from serotonergic drugs and features clonus and fever, not isolated hypertension.

quiz.q: A patient who has taken prednisone 15 mg daily for a year is vomiting with a BP of 82/48 that does not improve when you elevate the legs. What should you tell the receiving hospital?
choices: She may be in adrenal crisis from chronic steroid suppression and may need hospital steroids
She is dehydrated and needs oral fluids
She has a steroid allergy
Prednisone is causing her hypotension directly
quiz.why: Months of daily steroids suppress the body's own stress hormone production, so illness or injury can produce hypotension that fluids and positioning alone do not fix. Naming the possibility in the handoff is the intervention an EMT can make.

quiz.q: A patient's counter holds carbidopa-levodopa dosed five times a day, and the family says he has not taken it since yesterday morning. What should you expect?
choices: Hyperactivity and insomnia
Increasing rigidity, falls, and difficulty swallowing
Hypoglycemia
No effect; missed doses are harmless
quiz.why: Parkinson's medication dosed that frequently is holding movement and swallowing together hour by hour, so missed doses produce rigidity, fall risk and aspiration risk. The schedule itself is the clue to how tight the control is.

quiz.q: A bottle of 90 metformin tablets was filled 30 days ago and 78 tablets remain. What is the most useful conclusion?
choices: The patient is overusing the medication
The pharmacy made a filling error
The patient has taken only about 12 doses in 30 days, so adherence is poor
The count tells you nothing clinically useful
quiz.why: Twelve tablets gone in thirty days on a once or twice daily drug means the prescription is barely being taken. Fill date and remaining count are often the most useful information on the label.

quiz.q: An E cylinder reads 900 psi and you are running a nonrebreather at 12 L/min. Approximately how many minutes remain before the safe residual?
choices: About 8 minutes
About 45 minutes
About 30 minutes
About 16 minutes
quiz.why: 900 minus the 200 psi residual is 700, times the E cylinder constant of 0.28 is 196, divided by 12 L/min is about 16 minutes. Forgetting to subtract the residual or using the D cylinder constant of 0.16 produces the other answers.

quiz.q: You need 1.5 mg of a drug and the vial reads 0.5 mg/mL. What volume do you draw, and what is the decimal trap here?
choices: 3 mL; confusing 1.5 with 0.15 would underdose tenfold
0.3 mL; confusing 1.5 with 0.15 would underdose tenfold
0.75 mL; confusing 0.5 with 5 would overdose tenfold
7.5 mL; confusing 0.5 with 0.05 would overdose tenfold
quiz.why: 1.5 divided by 0.5 is 3 mL. Reading the ordered dose as 0.15 mg would yield 0.3 mL, a tenfold underdose, which is why leading zeros and spoken read-backs exist.

quiz.q: Which statement about the two epinephrine concentrations is correct?
choices: 0.1 mg/mL is the intramuscular anaphylaxis concentration
1 mg/mL delivers 0.3 mg in 0.3 mL and is the intramuscular anaphylaxis concentration
Both concentrations deliver the same dose in the same volume
1 mg/mL is ten times weaker than 0.1 mg/mL
quiz.why: The 1 mg/mL solution, formerly labeled 1:1,000, gives 0.3 mg in 0.3 mL for intramuscular anaphylaxis. The 0.1 mg/mL cardiac-arrest concentration is ten times more dilute and would require 3 mL for the same dose.

quiz.q: A 6 kg infant has anaphylaxis. Your kit holds a 0.15 mg auto-injector, a 0.3 mg auto-injector, and a 1 mg/mL vial with syringes under protocol. What is correct?
choices: Use half of the 0.3 mg auto-injector
Use the 0.15 mg auto-injector; it is close enough
Draw 0.06 mg, which is 0.06 mL, from the 1 mg/mL vial
Withhold epinephrine until ALS arrives
quiz.why: At 0.01 mg/kg, a 6 kg infant needs 0.06 mg, which is 0.06 mL of the 1 mg/mL solution. Auto-injector needles are too long and the fixed doses too large for an infant under 7.5 kg, and an auto-injector cannot be split.

quiz.q: An anaphylactic patient on carvedilol has received two doses of epinephrine without improvement. What should you expect the hospital to add, and what is your role now?
choices: Diphenhydramine alone, while you stop epinephrine
Oral steroids, while you cancel ALS
A third auto-injector given intravenously by you
Glucagon 1 to 5 mg intravenously; continue ventilation support, request ALS, and report the beta blocker
quiz.why: Glucagon raises cardiac output through a receptor the beta blocker does not occupy, which is the definitive answer for a beta-blocked patient. Antihistamines and steroids are slow adjuncts, and EMTs never push an intramuscular concentration intravenously.

quiz.q: An auto-injector fires into your index finger during a struggling pediatric injection. The fingertip turns white, cold and numb. What do you do?
choices: Keep the hand warm, seek emergency evaluation, and note the time of injection
Apply ice to reduce swelling
Inject the other side to balance the effect
Wrap the finger tightly and finish the shift
quiz.why: Epinephrine clamps down the small digital arteries, so the treatment is warmth and prompt emergency evaluation with the time documented. Ice and tight wrapping both worsen the ischemia.

quiz.q: You are bagging a suspected fentanyl overdose and the chest is so rigid that almost no air moves despite a good seal, an oral airway and two-person technique. What is the best course?
choices: Stop ventilating and perform abdominal thrusts for an obstruction
Continue aggressive two-person ventilation and give naloxone, which reverses chest wall rigidity
Insert a supraglottic airway yourself and increase pressure
Assume death and stop resuscitation
quiz.why: High-dose fentanyl can stiffen chest and abdominal muscles so that bagging feels obstructed when the airway is actually open. Naloxone reverses the rigidity, and abdominal thrusts are for a foreign body, which this is not.

quiz.q: A hospice patient on high-dose morphine for bone pain is breathing 5 times a minute. Family says this began after her scheduled dose. What is the safest approach?
choices: Give the full naloxone dose immediately to restore alertness
Withhold all treatment because she is in hospice
Ventilate with a bag-valve mask and give the smallest effective naloxone amount, waiting the full 2 to 3 minutes between doses
Give naloxone and then discharge her to family care
quiz.why: Full reversal strips away the only thing controlling severe pain and precipitates violent withdrawal, while inadequate ventilation is what actually kills. Hospice status does not remove the duty to treat a reversible respiratory emergency, though goals of care should be clarified.

quiz.q: A responder hesitates to touch a patient because of street fentanyl on the scene. What is accurate?
choices: Skin contact with fentanyl reliably causes responder overdose
Naloxone should be given to all responders prophylactically
The entire scene requires hazmat decontamination before patient contact
Gloves and avoiding face contact are sufficient; skin contact does not cause overdose, and delay harms the patient
quiz.why: Casual skin contact with fentanyl does not produce responder overdose, and standard gloves are adequate. Scene-wide hesitation delays the ventilation that is actually keeping the patient alive.

quiz.q: A patient with chest pain took three of his own nitroglycerin tablets from a bottle opened 18 months ago and kept in his truck, with no relief. BP is 132/80. What is the most useful conclusion?
choices: The tablets may be inert from heat, light and age; treat as ongoing cardiac pain and consider a fresh supply per protocol
The pain is definitely not cardiac
He is allergic to nitroglycerin
He should take three more of the same tablets
quiz.why: Sublingual tablets degrade with heat, light and time, so an old bottle in a hot vehicle may deliver nothing. Concluding the pain is not cardiac because degraded tablets failed is exactly the trap, and exceeding three doses is not the fix.

quiz.q: A hypotensive patient in cardiac arrest is about to be defibrillated and has a nitroglycerin patch on the left chest. What do you do?
choices: Leave it and place pads elsewhere without removing it
Remove the patch with a gloved hand, wipe the skin, then place pads
Defibrillate through the patch to save time
Apply the pads directly over the patch for better contact
quiz.why: The metallic backing of a patch can arc and burn the skin during defibrillation, and the patch is still delivering a vasodilator. Gloved removal and wiping the skin takes seconds and removes both problems.

quiz.q: A patient with asthma, nasal polyps and a history of severe wheezing after ibuprofen presents with crushing chest pain. What about aspirin?
choices: Give the full 324 mg; the reaction was to ibuprofen, not aspirin
Give 81 mg as a test dose
Withhold aspirin; this is aspirin-exacerbated respiratory disease, a genuine contraindication
Give it with an antihistamine to prevent the reaction
quiz.why: The triad of asthma, nasal polyps and NSAID-triggered wheezing predicts a severe aspirin reaction because aspirin and ibuprofen share the same mechanism. Test doses and antihistamine premedication are not field practice.

quiz.q: An unresponsive hypoglycemic patient with a glucose of 27 mg/dL has no gag reflex. Your service carries intranasal glucagon. What is the correct sequence?
choices: Place glucose gel in the cheek, then give glucagon
Wait for ALS without treatment since glucagon works slowly
Give glucagon and then sit the patient up to speed absorption
Manage the airway and ventilate as needed, give glucagon 3 mg intranasally, position for vomiting, request ALS, and recheck glucose
quiz.why: The airway comes first, glucagon is the treatment available without an IV or a swallow, and vomiting is the expected side effect so positioning and suction matter. Gel in the cheek of a patient with no gag reflex is aspiration with extra steps.

quiz.q: Twenty minutes after intramuscular glucagon, a malnourished patient with alcoholic liver disease is still unresponsive with a glucose of 34 mg/dL. Why?
choices: Glucagon releases stored liver glycogen, and in liver disease or starvation those stores are empty, so only intravenous dextrose will work
The glucagon dose was too low and should be tripled
Glucagon only works in type 1 diabetes
The glucometer is reading the sensor, not the blood
quiz.why: Glucagon unlocks a storeroom rather than delivering sugar, so it fails when glycogen stores are depleted by alcohol use, liver disease or starvation. The answer is ALS or hospital dextrose, not more glucagon.

quiz.q: A hypoglycemic patient wearing an insulin pump is now awake and improving. What should you do about the pump?
choices: Remove the infusion set yourself immediately
Ask the patient or family to suspend or disconnect it, and document the time it was stopped
Ignore it; pumps stop automatically during hypoglycemia
Increase the basal rate to stabilize the reading
quiz.why: The pump keeps delivering insulin unless someone stops it, and the patient or family knows the device. Pressing unfamiliar buttons or pulling infusion sets yourself is outside scope in most systems and risks making things worse.

quiz.q: A student asks why an EMT in one state can give nebulized albuterol but an EMT in another cannot. What is the most accurate explanation?
choices: Federal law lists every EMT medication identically nationwide
It depends on the ambulance manufacturer
The national scope model is a floor; each state, then each medical director's protocol, then the individual credential determines what you actually carry
It depends only on whether the service is paid or volunteer
quiz.why: Four layers stack: the national scope model, state law, the medical director's protocol, and your own credential. There is no federal drug list for EMTs, and funding model has nothing to do with scope.

quiz.q: A CPAP patient in pulmonary edema is being moved from the stretcher to the hospital bed. When is the highest-risk moment?
choices: During the first minute of application
After the patient is settled in the bed
While the pressure is being titrated from 5 to 10
When the mask is taken off for the transfer
quiz.why: Removing the mask drops the airway pressure that was holding the air sacs open, and the crash classically happens during a brief transfer. Keeping CPAP on through hallway moves and the switch to the hospital bed prevents it.

quiz.q: Which practice is the most effective structural defense against look-alike medication errors?
choices: Stocking only one concentration of a drug and removing look-alike packaging from the bag
Reminding crews to be more careful at shift briefing
Posting a list of look-alike names in the station
Disciplining any EMT who reports a near miss
quiz.why: Removing the wrong option from the bag stops the error at the source, while reminders and posted lists depend on attention under pressure. Disciplining near-miss reports destroys the data that prevents the next one.

quiz.q: You realize on the way to the hospital that you gave aspirin to a patient who told you she has a bleeding ulcer. What is the correct order of actions?
choices: Document it quietly and let the hospital discover it on chart review
Reassess and treat the patient, tell your partner, tell the receiving nurse and physician explicitly at handoff, document facts, and file the report
Ask the patient not to mention it and monitor her
Correct the chart to remove the entry and continue transport
quiz.why: Patient assessment comes first, then explicit disclosure to the receiving team, then factual documentation and a report. Concealment or altering a record turns a treatable error into a far more serious problem.

quiz.q: An EMT knowingly works a shift while impaired and gives a medication incorrectly. Under just culture, how is this handled?
choices: Consoled as human error
Coached as at-risk behavior
Disciplined as reckless behavior
Ignored because no harm resulted
quiz.why: Reckless behavior is a conscious disregard of a substantial risk and is the one category just culture assigns to discipline. Human error gets consoling and at-risk drift gets coaching, and absence of harm does not change the classification.

quiz.q: During a chaotic scene an EMT is interrupted mid-preparation by a radio call and then gives the wrong strength auto-injector. Which contributing factor does this best illustrate?
choices: Deliberate protocol violation
An expired medication supply
Inadequate initial training
Interruption during medication preparation
quiz.why: Interruption during preparation is one of the best-documented sources of medication error, which is why the three checks are spaced and the dose is spoken aloud. Nothing here suggests intent, training gaps or an expiration problem.
